Description: Follow-up for unexplained falls, balance disturbance, intermittent apparent syncope, and choking with swallowing.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient has experienced multiple recent falls, reportedly approximately eight during December and another the preceding night. A companion witnessed the last episode, describing a sudden collapse with a very brief period of altered awareness. There was no reported warning with palpitations or lightheadedness and no clear seizure-like activity or incontinence. The patient has soreness of the head and neck after the fall, longstanding sensory disturbances, gait imbalance, and occasional unusual sensation of being upside down. Prior neurological and cardiovascular workup has not identified a single cause. He increasingly needs an object to hold for stability, and therapy has suggested a wheelchair for longer distances. He also reports significant choking or coughing with initial swallows of food or liquids despite prior swallowing evaluation and dietary adjustments.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Blood pressure approximately 134/80 supine and 128/80 seated, without significant positional decline. Posterior scalp examination shows tenderness without visible wound. Examination was directed toward balance, injury, and orthostatic symptoms.
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Recurrent falls, possibly multifactorial, in the setting of neurologic ataxia and polypharmacy. Previous cardiac evaluation has not demonstrated a clear structural or arrhythmic cause. Obtain EKG and additional blood tests and review medications that may contribute. Support use of a wheelchair to reduce injury risk.
2. Bone protection after frequent falls. Check vitamin D and obtain DEXA scanning to assess for osteoporosis.
3. Swallowing difficulty. Continue precautions and follow-up of prior swallowing assessment; mixed consistencies and liquids can trigger coughing.
4. Medication refills were reviewed, including etodolac and allergy therapies. Patient reports penicillin and caffeine sensitivity.
5. Follow-up in three to four months, sooner for further injury, prolonged loss of consciousness, or worsening dysphagia.
